title: Difficulty swallowing in a 65-year-old retired chef
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 65-year-old retired chef in general practice with 3 months of progressive dysphagia to solids, weight loss and anorexia. She has long-standing reflux, takes naproxen regularly, is obese and is a heavy smoker. The candidate then interprets her blood tests, gastroscopy and biopsy report and staging CT, recognises a distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma arising in Barrett's oesophagus, and plans urgent specialist referral, nutrition support, how to tell her the news, and safety netting.
focus: Telling oropharyngeal from oesophageal dysphagia and recognising the alarm features of oesophageal cancer in general practice
stem: You are a GP in a suburban general practice. Samantha, a 65-year-old retired chef, has made an appointment because she has been having difficulty swallowing.
tasks: Take a focused history from Samantha and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Samantha's blood test results, her gastroscopy and biopsy report and her CT report. You will be asked to hand over to a colleague, give your diagnosis and differentials, outline your management, and explain the result and safety netting to Samantha (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Samantha, a 65-year-old retired chef. You are friendly but low in mood. Cooking and eating have been your life, and not being able to enjoy food is really getting to you. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Well, doctor, I've been having some trouble eating..."

The swallowing problem (give only when asked):

  • Food feels like it gets stuck in the middle of your chest, behind the breastbone (point to the middle of your sternum).
  • If asked: starting a swallow is no problem. Food goes down from your mouth fine and then sticks lower down.
  • Only solid food is a problem. Liquids such as soups and broths go down easily.
  • If asked how it makes you feel: "It's been awful. I can't enjoy eating any more, and that's very hard for me as a chef."
  • It started about 3 months ago and came on gradually. At first it was only with big pieces of meat or bread. Now it happens whenever you eat solid food. It has been steadily getting worse. You have never had anything like it before.
  • It is there every time you eat solids; it does not come and go.
  • You now chew everything very carefully and have switched to soft foods and soups.
  • If asked: changing position (sitting up, lying down) makes no difference.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • You have lost about 5 kg over the 3 months without trying. Your clothes are looser.
  • You have gone off your food and don't feel like eating.
  • You are tired all the time.
  • You still get heartburn and acid reflux, although the pantoprazole helps most of the time.
  • It hurts a little as solid food goes down.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Fevers or night sweats.
  • Cough, coughing or choking when you eat or drink, coughing up blood, or a hoarse voice.
  • Nausea or vomiting. Food or fluid coming back up into your mouth.
  • Bad breath, or a gurgling noise in your throat or neck when you swallow.
  • Food you ate hours earlier, or undigested food, coming back up, including at night.
  • Vomiting blood, or black tarry poo.
  • Feeling full early in a meal.
  • Any change in your bowels.
  • Weakness, numbness or tingling, problems with your speech or face, or loss of control of your bladder or bowels.

Context (only if asked):

  • Reflux for about 15 years. If asked about Barrett's oesophagus or a camera test: "No, I've never had a camera test. Nobody has ever mentioned Barrett's. My old GP just gave me the tablets."
  • Never had a stroke or any nerve, muscle or connective tissue problem (no scleroderma, no Raynaud's, no Parkinson's).
  • Never had stomach or gut surgery, radiotherapy to the chest or neck, or swallowed anything caustic such as bleach.
  • Never been told you have a hiatus hernia.
  • Never had cancer.
  • If asked about your weight: "I've always been on the heavy side. The nurse says I'm overweight."

Past medical history: reflux (GORD) for about 15 years. Osteoarthritis in both knees.

Medications:

  • Pantoprazole 40 mg once a day.
  • Naproxen 500 mg twice a day for your knees, for the past couple of years.
  • Nothing else.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your father had reflux. No one in the family has had cancer of the food pipe, stomach or bowel.

Social history:

  • You live with your husband and are fully independent.
  • Your two adult daughters visit every weekend.
  • You smoke about 40 cigarettes a day (two packs of 20) and have done for the past 20 years, since you were 45. You still smoke.
  • If asked why you started so late: "I started when I was working long shifts in the restaurant kitchen in my mid-40s."
  • A glass of red wine every night with dinner.
  • No recreational drugs.
  • If asked about your diet: "Honestly, I cook a lot of rich food. Not much fruit and veg."
  • If asked: you are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I wondered if my reflux has just got worse."
  • Concern: you miss enjoying food, and you are quietly worried it might be something serious.
  • Expectation: you want to find out what is wrong and be able to eat properly again.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Do you think it's just my reflux playing up?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: alert, comfortable at rest, smells of cigarette smoke. Weight 92 kg (practice record 3 months ago: 97 kg), height 165 cm, BMI 34.
  • Observations: HR 84 regular, BP 138/84, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C.
  • Hands: nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers. No clubbing or koilonychia.
  • Eyes: mild conjunctival pallor. No scleral icterus.
  • Mouth and throat: good dentition, moist mucous membranes, no oral ulcers, candida or masses. Palate rises symmetrically, tongue protrudes midline with no wasting or fasciculation, voice normal.
  • Water swallow (if asked to observe a sip of water): swallows without coughing, choking or change in voice.
  • Neck: no cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes (including the left supraclavicular fossa). Thyroid not enlarged. No neck mass.
  • Chest: mildly reduced air entry throughout, no crackles or wheeze. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen: obese, soft and non-tender. No epigastric mass. Liver and spleen not palpable. No ascites.
  • Neurological screen (if done): normal limb power, sensation and reflexes; no facial asymmetry or dysarthria.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Samantha's identity, gains consent and asks whether she is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Uses plain language and responds with empathy to how hard the swallowing problem is for her as a chef.
History
Characterises the dysphagia:

kids.x: Level and initiation: food sticks in the middle of the chest after swallowing, with no difficulty starting a swallow.
Solids or liquids: solids only; liquids (soups, broths) go down easily.
Onset and progression: 3 months, gradual and worsening, at first only large pieces and now whenever she eats solids; never before.
Pattern and adaptations: constant rather than intermittent, no change with position; she chews carefully and has changed to soft foods.

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms:
check.d: Source mark scheme: features asked from at least two systems.

kids.x: Constitutional: 5 kg weight loss over 3 months without trying, loss of appetite and fatigue.
Upper GI: heartburn and reflux, and pain on swallowing; no nausea, vomiting, regurgitation, early satiety, vomiting blood or black stools.
Respiratory and ENT: no cough or choking with eating, no haemoptysis, no hoarseness.
Systemic and lower GI: no fever or sweats, no change in bowel habit.

check.x: Screens for causes of oropharyngeal dysphagia: previous stroke, weakness, sensory change or incontinence, and neuromuscular or connective tissue disease (for example myasthenia, Parkinson's disease, scleroderma).

Asks context questions about structural causes: how long she has had reflux and whether she has had a gastroscopy or been told of Barrett's oesophagus; hiatus hernia; previous GI surgery, radiotherapy or caustic ingestion; previous cancer.
check.d: Award for at least three context questions (source mark scheme).

check.x: Takes the past medical history: GORD for about 15 years and knee osteoarthritis.
Takes a medication and allergy history: pantoprazole, regular naproxen (an NSAID that can injure the oesophagus and cause a stricture), no allergies.
Takes a family history: father had reflux; no family history of oesophageal, stomach or bowel cancer.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Quantifies smoking: about 40 cigarettes a day for 20 years (40 pack-years), still smoking.
Quantifies alcohol: a glass of red wine every night; no other drugs.
Living situation, function and diet: lives independently with her husband, daughters visit every weekend, diet low in fruit and vegetables.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks her reflux may have got worse, misses enjoying food, wants to know what is wrong and to eat normally again; and answers her question honestly: this is not simply reflux and needs an urgent gastroscopy.
Examination
Asks for vital signs, weight and BMI, and compares the weight with the practice record (97 kg three months ago, 92 kg today).
Inspects generally and examines the hands and eyes: wasting, pallor, jaundice, clubbing, koilonychia and nicotine staining.
Examines the neck for cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes, including the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node.
Examines the mouth and oropharynx, checks the lower cranial nerves (palate, tongue, voice) and observes her swallowing a sip of water.
check.d: Award for the mouth plus either the cranial nerve check or the water swallow.

check.x: Examines the abdomen for an epigastric mass, hepatomegaly and ascites.
Listens to the chest, and summarises the examination: objective weight loss and mild pallor, with no lymphadenopathy, abdominal mass or neurological signs.
Interpretation

Interprets the bloods: microcytic anaemia with low ferritin and transferrin saturation (iron deficiency, most likely slow blood loss from the oesophagus, with naproxen and poor intake contributing); low albumin (poor nutrition); normal liver tests and renal function.
Interprets the gastroscopy: an ulcerated mass narrowing the distal oesophagus within a long segment of salmon-coloured (Barrett's) mucosa, with a normal stomach and duodenum.
Interprets the histology: invasive adenocarcinoma in the mass, and Barrett's oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia) with high-grade dysplasia in the segment above it.
Interprets the CT: distal oesophageal tumour with enlarged paraoesophageal nodes and no distant metastases on CT, so locoregional disease that still needs PET-CT to complete staging.

States the diagnosis as adenocarcinoma of the distal oesophagus arising in Barrett's oesophagus, justified by progressive solids-only dysphagia with no difficulty initiating, weight loss and anorexia, long-standing GORD, obesity and heavy smoking, and the results.
Gives differentials with a feature for or against each:
check.d: Also credit other reasonable differentials (oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, extrinsic compression from lung cancer, eosinophilic oesophagitis) given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Peptic stricture: for: long-standing GORD and naproxen; against: rapid progression with weight loss, and a malignant mass at endoscopy.
Oesophageal pouch or diverticulum: against: food sticks in the mid-chest rather than the neck; no gurgling, halitosis, delayed regurgitation of undigested food or cough; no pouch at endoscopy.

Motility disorder such as achalasia: against: solids only with liquids easy (achalasia usually affects solids and liquids from the start), no regurgitation of undigested food, and an obstructing mass at endoscopy.

check.x: Management
Gives a brief warning shot, then says clearly in plain words that the biopsy shows cancer of the lower food pipe, pauses and responds to her emotion.
Ensures urgent referral to the upper GI (oesophagogastric) surgical team and multidisciplinary team, phones to confirm the appointment, and links her with a cancer care coordinator.

Explains the next steps: PET-CT (and possibly endoscopic ultrasound) to complete staging, a treatment decision at the MDT meeting, and that for disease like hers treatment is usually chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery if she is fit enough.
check.d: Do not require a named regimen.

check.x: Addresses nutrition: urgent dietitian referral, soft, moist or liquid high-energy food with oral nutritional supplements, and regular weighing.

Reviews medicines: stops naproxen and uses paracetamol (liquid or dispersible if needed), continues pantoprazole, and plans iron replacement (IV iron is a sensible choice with dysphagia and treatment ahead).
Offers smoking cessation support (brief advice, Quitline, pharmacotherapy) and advises cutting down alcohol, framed as getting her as fit as possible for treatment (CT shows emphysema).
Offers support: involves her husband and daughters if she wishes, and gives written information and the Cancer Council 13 11 20 number.
Safety netting

Names at least three specific red flags in plain words, each linked to where to go: cannot swallow fluids or saliva, or food stuck and will not pass (ED same day); vomiting blood, black stools, feeling faint, or sudden or severe chest pain or breathlessness (call 000/ED); fever, or coughing or choking when eating or drinking (same-day GP or urgent review).
Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week (weight, eating, iron, coping) and again after the specialist appointment, and stays in contact with the MDT and cancer care coordinator.

part2.lead: Samantha had blood tests on the day you saw her, and you referred her for an urgent gastroscopy, which was done 9 days later. The gastroenterologist took biopsies and arranged a staging CT, and told her you would go through the results. She has come back today. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Samantha has not yet been told the biopsy result. When the candidate explains it, go quiet for a moment, then ask once: "So it really is cancer? Will I be able to eat properly again?"

You become calmer if the candidate gives you a clear plan and tells you who will support you. If the candidate uses jargon (Barrett's, adenocarcinoma, staging, MDT) without explaining it, ask once what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at the practice on the day of the first visit.
handover.model:
• Read: haemoglobin 112 with an MCV of 78: a mild microcytic anaemia. Ferritin 12, iron 6 and transferrin saturation 7% confirm iron deficiency. Albumin 33 is low. White cells and platelets normal. Electrolytes, renal function, calcium and liver tests normal.
  • For Samantha: iron deficiency in a 65-year-old woman with dysphagia points to slow blood loss from the ulcerated oesophageal tumour, with regular naproxen and poor intake contributing; it explains her fatigue and is another alarm feature. The low albumin fits poor nutrition and weight loss. Normal liver tests and calcium do not exclude metastases, but are reassuring.
  • What it changes: she needs iron replacement (oral tablets are hard with dysphagia and often poorly tolerated, so IV iron is a sensible option), dietitian input, and normal renal function means contrast imaging and chemotherapy are not limited by her kidneys.

handover.label: Gastroscopy and biopsy report
handover.result:
Procedure: gastroscopy under sedation, 9 days after the GP visit.

Clinical details: 65-year-old woman with 3 months of progressive dysphagia to solids, 5 kg weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia. Long-standing GORD on pantoprazole, regular naproxen, current smoker. No previous gastroscopy.

Findings:

  • Oesophagus: upper and mid oesophagus normal. Salmon-coloured columnar-type mucosa extends from 33 cm to the gastro-oesophageal junction at 39 cm from the incisors (Prague C4M6). Within this segment, from 34 to 38 cm, there is an ulcerated, friable, exophytic mass involving about three-quarters of the circumference and narrowing the lumen. The standard gastroscope passed through with gentle pressure. No hiatus hernia.
  • Stomach: normal, including the cardia on retroflexion. No mass or ulcer.
  • Duodenum: normal to the second part.

Biopsies: 8 from the mass; separate biopsies from the columnar-lined segment above it.

Histology:

  • Mass: invasive adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated. HER2 testing requested.
  • Columnar-lined segment: intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and high-grade dysplasia, consistent with Barrett's oesophagus.

Conclusion: distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma arising in a long segment of Barrett's oesophagus. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis arranged for staging; referred to the upper GI multidisciplinary team.
handover.model:
• Read: a 6 cm segment of salmon-coloured columnar mucosa above the gastro-oesophageal junction (Barrett's), with an ulcerated, friable mass from 34 to 38 cm narrowing three-quarters of the lumen. Stomach and duodenum normal. Biopsies: invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma in the mass; intestinal metaplasia with high-grade dysplasia in the segment above.
  • For Samantha: adenocarcinoma of the distal oesophagus arising in Barrett's oesophagus, the end of a sequence driven by 15 years of reflux, with obesity and smoking adding to the risk. The narrowed lumen explains the progressive solids-only dysphagia, and the ulcerated, friable surface explains the iron deficiency.
  • What it changes: she needs staging and an urgent upper GI MDT review. HER2 status (with MMR and PD-L1 testing) guides treatment if the disease turns out to be advanced or comes back. The high-grade dysplasia in the rest of the Barrett's segment will be part of the surgical or endoscopic plan.

handover.label: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
handover.result:
Examination: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (portal venous phase).

Clinical details: biopsy-proven distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Staging.

Comparison: none available.

Findings:

  • Oesophagus: asymmetric wall thickening of the distal oesophagus over about 4 cm, maximum thickness 15 mm, ending just above the gastro-oesophageal junction, with mild stranding of the surrounding fat. Fat planes with the aorta, left atrium and diaphragmatic crura are preserved.
  • Lymph nodes: two enlarged paraoesophageal nodes beside the tumour, 11 mm and 12 mm in short axis. No enlarged supraclavicular, other mediastinal, coeliac or retroperitoneal nodes.
  • Lungs and pleura: mild centrilobular emphysema in both upper lobes. No pulmonary nodule, mass or consolidation. No pleural effusion.
  • Liver: no focal lesion. Mild diffuse fatty infiltration.
  • Other abdomen and pelvis: adrenal glands, spleen, pancreas and kidneys normal. No ascites or peritoneal nodularity. Pelvis unremarkable.
  • Bones: no lytic or sclerotic lesion. Degenerative change in the spine.

Conclusion: distal oesophageal tumour with likely involved paraoesophageal lymph nodes. No distant metastases on CT. PET-CT is suggested to complete staging.
handover.model:
• Read: contrast CT showing a 4 cm thickened distal oesophagus with preserved fat planes to the aorta, heart and crura, two enlarged paraoesophageal nodes, and no liver, lung, adrenal, peritoneal or bone metastases. Upper lobe emphysema; no lung mass.
  • For Samantha: locoregional disease (the tumour and nearby nodes), with no distant spread seen on CT and no sign of invasion into nearby structures. CT is not enough to stage it fully. The absence of a lung mass also argues against extrinsic compression from lung cancer in a 40 pack-year smoker.
  • What it changes: she is potentially curable, so staging is completed (PET-CT, and possibly endoscopic ultrasound, as the team decides) before an MDT treatment decision. The emphysema matters for her fitness for surgery and is one more reason to stop smoking now.

ask: You are now calling the upper gastrointestinal surgical registrar at the local hospital to expedite Samantha's review. Please give an ISBAR handover of Samantha, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Samantha now, here in general practice.
Samantha has not yet been told the biopsy result. Please explain it to her briefly, then tell her what to watch out for.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP, practice; Samantha, 65, retired chef.
  • Situation: biopsy-proven distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma; requesting urgent upper GI review and MDT discussion.
  • Background: 3 months of progressive dysphagia to solids, 5 kg weight loss, anorexia, fatigue. GORD for 15 years, never scoped; naproxen; obese (BMI 34); 40 pack-years, still smoking; nightly wine.
  • Assessment: Hb 112, MCV 78, ferritin 12: iron deficiency anaemia; albumin 33; renal and liver tests normal. Gastroscopy: ulcerated mass at 34 to 38 cm narrowing the lumen in a C4M6 Barrett's segment; adenocarcinoma, high-grade dysplasia above, HER2 pending. CT: paraoesophageal nodes, no distant metastases, emphysema.
  • Recommendation: urgent clinic appointment and MDT discussion; PET-CT to complete staging; I am arranging a dietitian and iron replacement.

Most likely: adenocarcinoma of the distal oesophagus arising in Barrett's oesophagus. Rapidly progressive dysphagia, first to large pieces and then to all solids, with no difficulty initiating (so oesophageal rather than oropharyngeal) and solids only with liquids easy (so mechanical rather than motility), weight loss and anorexia; risk factors of long-standing GORD, obesity and 40 pack-years of smoking; confirmed on biopsy.

  • Peptic stricture: for: GORD, naproxen. Against: rapid progression, weight loss, malignant mass.
  • Oesophageal pouch or diverticulum: against: food sticks in the mid-chest rather than the neck; no gurgling, halitosis, delayed regurgitation of undigested food or cough; no pouch at endoscopy.
  • Achalasia or another motility disorder: against: solids only with liquids easy (achalasia usually affects solids and liquids from the start), no regurgitation of undigested food, obstructing mass at endoscopy.
  • Extrinsic compression from lung cancer: for: smoker. Against: no cough or haemoptysis, no lung mass on CT.

1. Urgent referral: confirm the upper GI surgical and MDT referral and the appointment date; link her with a cancer care coordinator.
  2. Staging and treatment by the team: PET-CT (and possibly endoscopic ultrasound), then an MDT decision; for locoregional disease usually chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, then oesophagectomy if fit.
  3. Nutrition: urgent dietitian referral, soft, moist or liquid high-energy food, oral supplements, weigh regularly.
  4. Medicines: stop naproxen, use paracetamol (liquid or dispersible); continue pantoprazole; iron replacement, IV iron a sensible option.
  5. Prehabilitation: smoking cessation (Quitline, pharmacotherapy), cut down alcohol, stay active.
  6. Support: involve husband and daughters if she wishes, written information, Cancer Council 13 11 20, psychological support, GP management plan.
  7. Follow-up: GP review within a week and after the specialist appointment.

• Breaking the news: brief warning shot, then in plain words: the biopsy shows cancer in the lower part of the food pipe. Pause and acknowledge her feelings.
  • Her question: confirms it is cancer; it is not her fault. The scan so far shows no spread beyond nearby glands; once the last scan is done, the team hopes to offer treatment aimed at cure. The dietitian and the team can help her keep eating.
  • Go to ED the same day if she can't swallow fluids or saliva, or food sticks and won't pass. Call 000 or go to ED for vomiting blood, black stools, feeling faint, or sudden severe chest pain or breathlessness; see a doctor the same day for fever or coughing when she eats or drinks.

ddx.dx: Adenocarcinoma of the distal oesophagus arising in Barrett's oesophagus
ddx.for: Progressive solids-only dysphagia over 3 months with no difficulty initiating, 5 kg weight loss and anorexia, 15 years of GORD, obesity and 40 pack-years, and an ulcerated distal mass with adenocarcinoma in a Barrett's segment.
Long-standing GORD, regular naproxen and dysphagia to solids only.
ddx.against: Rapid progression with weight loss, anorexia and iron deficiency, and a malignant mass on biopsy.

ddx.for: 40 pack-years, nightly alcohol and a diet low in fruit and vegetables.
ddx.against: The tumour is distal, within a Barrett's segment, and the histology is adenocarcinoma.

ddx.dx: Oesophageal pouch or diverticulum (including pharyngeal pouch)
ddx.for: Older age and dysphagia to solids.
ddx.against: Food sticks in the mid-chest rather than the throat, and she has no halitosis, delayed regurgitation or cough.

ddx.dx: Achalasia or another oesophageal motility disorder
ddx.against: Solids only with liquids easy, no regurgitation of undigested food or night-time cough, and an obstructing mass at endoscopy.

ddx.dx: Extrinsic compression of the oesophagus from lung cancer or mediastinal nodes
ddx.against: No cough, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no lung mass or bulky mediastinal nodes on CT.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate orders tests or refers in Part 1, say the results will come in Part 2. Whatever the candidate planned, the bloods were taken on the day, the urgent gastroscopy was done, and the gastroenterologist arranged the CT. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Samantha asks her one question once while the candidate explains the result.

The source mark scheme rewards breadth: at least three context questions (item 8) and associated features from at least two systems (item 6). The key discriminating questions are where the food sticks, whether starting a swallow is difficult, solids versus liquids, and the progression with weight loss.

A high-performing candidate separates oesophageal from oropharyngeal dysphagia early, establishes progressive solids-only dysphagia with weight loss and anorexia as alarm features, quantifies her smoking and finds the naproxen and never-scoped reflux, and examines for objective weight loss, pallor, Virchow's node and an epigastric mass or liver. In Part 2 they read the iron deficiency, the Barrett's-associated adenocarcinoma and the locoregional CT correctly, break the news clearly and kindly, and plan urgent MDT referral, staging, nutrition, medicine changes, smoking cessation and specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic reflux history, misses the weight loss or smoking, does not ask about initiation or solids versus liquids, or in Part 2 avoids the word cancer, offers a PPI dose increase as the plan, forgets nutrition, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis

Samantha has an adenocarcinoma of the distal oesophagus arising in Barrett's oesophagus. Her history is the classic picture of a mechanical oesophageal obstruction: food sticks in the mid-chest after swallowing, there is no difficulty starting a swallow, only solids are affected, and it has progressed over 3 months from large pieces to all solids. Weight loss, anorexia and fatigue are alarm features. Her risk factors for adenocarcinoma are 15 years of GORD (never investigated), obesity and 40 pack-years of smoking. Her nightly alcohol and low fruit and vegetable intake matter more for squamous cell carcinoma and for her general health.

Approach to dysphagia

Swallowing has oral, pharyngeal and oesophageal phases.

  • Oropharyngeal dysphagia: difficulty starting a swallow, with solids and liquids, choking, coughing or nasal regurgitation. Causes are neuromuscular (stroke, tumour, Parkinson's disease, dementia, myasthenia gravis) or structural (compression, pharyngeal pouch, also called Zenker's diverticulum).
  • Oesophageal dysphagia: food sticks after swallowing. Solids and liquids from the start suggest a motility disorder (achalasia, scleroderma). Solids only, progressive, suggests a mechanical obstruction (stricture or cancer). Intermittent solid food bolus obstruction suggests a ring, web or eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm feature and needs urgent gastroscopy. Gastroscopy is the first test, because it allows biopsy.

Differentials that matter

  • Peptic stricture (GORD, NSAIDs) also causes solids-only dysphagia, but usually progresses slowly without weight loss.
  • Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) is more common in older men and causes halitosis, gurgling, delayed regurgitation of undigested food and cough; mid- and lower-oesophageal diverticula are rarer.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking, alcohol and a poor diet and usually sits in the upper or mid oesophagus; adenocarcinoma is linked to GORD, Barrett's oesophagus, obesity and smoking and sits distally.
  • Extrinsic compression from lung cancer or mediastinal nodes must be considered in a heavy smoker.

Interpreting the results

  • Bloods: iron deficiency anaemia from slow blood loss, with naproxen and poor intake contributing; low albumin from poor nutrition.
  • Gastroscopy and histology: a long segment of Barrett's oesophagus (Prague C4M6) with an ulcerated, narrowing mass; invasive adenocarcinoma, with high-grade dysplasia in the surrounding Barrett's mucosa.
  • CT: locoregional disease (tumour and paraoesophageal nodes) with no distant metastases on CT. CT alone does not complete staging; PET-CT (and often endoscopic ultrasound) follow.

Management

The Optimal Care Pathway for people with oesophagogastric cancer sets out what happens next: urgent referral to a specialist team that treats oesophagogastric cancer, completion of staging, and a treatment plan made at a multidisciplinary meeting, with a care coordinator. For locally advanced disease in a fit patient, treatment is usually chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy before oesophagectomy. Patients unfit for surgery, or with metastatic disease, are offered definitive chemoradiotherapy or palliative treatment, including measures to relieve dysphagia. The GP's role continues throughout:

  • Nutrition: malnutrition is common and worsens outcomes. Refer urgently to a dietitian, change food texture, add oral supplements and weigh her regularly.
  • Medicines: stop the NSAID (bleeding from an ulcerated tumour, and her reflux), use paracetamol, continue the PPI, and replace iron (oral tablets are hard to swallow and often poorly tolerated).
  • Prehabilitation: smoking cessation, less alcohol and staying active improve fitness for treatment. Her emphysema matters for surgery.
  • Support: break the news clearly and kindly, involve her family if she wishes, and give her Cancer Council (13 11 20) and psychological support.

Barrett's oesophagus

Barrett's oesophagus is the replacement of the squamous lining of the distal oesophagus by columnar mucosa with intestinal metaplasia, caused by chronic reflux. It is the precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, through low-grade and then high-grade dysplasia. Australian guidelines (Cancer Council Australia) recommend endoscopic surveillance of known Barrett's, and endoscopic treatment of dysplasia and early cancer. Long-standing reflux in an older patient with risk factors should prompt consideration of gastroscopy, even without alarm features.

Safety netting

An obstructing oesophageal tumour can become complete, bleed, or cause aspiration or a fistula. She should go to the ED the same day if she cannot swallow fluids or saliva or food will not pass, call 000 or go to the ED for vomiting blood, black stools, fainting, or sudden severe chest pain or breathlessness (perforation, a fistula or a cardiac event), and see a doctor the same day for fever or coughing with eating and drinking. Book GP review within a week and after the specialist appointment.
points: Oropharyngeal dysphagia is difficulty starting a swallow (with choking, coughing or nasal regurgitation); oesophageal dysphagia is food sticking after the swallow.
Solids and liquids from the start suggest a motility disorder; progressive solids-only dysphagia suggests a mechanical obstruction such as a stricture or cancer.
Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm feature and needs urgent gastroscopy with biopsy.

Long-standing GORD, Barrett's oesophagus, obesity and smoking are the risk factors for oesophageal adenocarcinoma (distal); smoking, alcohol and a poor diet are the risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma.
Iron deficiency in an older adult with upper GI symptoms suggests GI blood loss and is another alarm feature.

Once oesophageal cancer is diagnosed, the GP ensures urgent MDT referral and supports nutrition, medicines (stop NSAIDs, replace iron), smoking cessation and psychosocial care, and gives clear red flags for complete obstruction and bleeding.
